faq.q: Why does a steam iron work better?
faq.a: Water molecules slip between the fibres and break the weak bonds holding a crease, so the fabric softens faster and at a lower temperature than with dry heat.
asks: What does the steam do when ironing?

faq.a: The soleplate is the flat, smooth metal base of the iron. An element inside heats it, and holes in it let steam out onto the fabric.
asks: What is the bottom of an iron called?

faq.q: Why should ironed clothes cool before wearing?
faq.a: The new flat shape only locks in once the fibres cool and dry. Wearing warm, damp clothes straight away can put new creases in.
asks: Why do clothes crease again after ironing?

faq.q: Why do irons have different heat settings?
faq.a: Fibres soften at different temperatures. Cotton and linen need about 200 degrees, while nylon and polyester would melt, so they need a much cooler setting.

faq.q: How does an iron keep the right temperature?
faq.a: A thermostat, often a bimetal strip, switches the heating element off when the plate reaches the setting and on again when it cools.
asks: Why does the iron light go on and off?

facts: The hottest iron setting, for cotton and linen, is around 200 °C, while synthetics need about 110 to 150 °C.
Steam helps remove creases because water breaks the weak bonds between the chain molecules in fibres such as cotton.
